title: A generic class
summary: Give a class a type parameter, like <T>, so one class works for any type.

say.never: You already use generic classes: `ArrayList<Integer>` and `ArrayList<String>` are the same class holding different things. You can write your own. After the class name, put a **type parameter** in angle brackets, like `<T>`. `T` is a blank that stands for "some type, chosen later". Inside the class, use `T` anywhere you'd write a type: a field, a parameter, a return type.
say.bit: A **type parameter** `<T>` after the class name is a blank for a type. Use `T` for fields, parameters and return types.

say.never: When you *use* the class, you fill in the blank: `Box<String>` is a box of text, `Box<Integer>` a box of whole numbers. Java now knows what comes out, so `open()` gives a `String` with no extra work, and putting the wrong type in is an error before the program even runs. Like with `ArrayList`, the blank takes a class, so write `Integer` and `Double`, not `int` and `double`.
say.bit: `Box<String>` fills in T. Java checks the types for you. Use `Integer`/`Double`, not `int`/`double`.

say.never: A class can have several type parameters, separated by commas. Each is its own blank, so the two values can be different types. By habit they're single capital letters: `T` for "type", `K` and `V` for "key" and "value", or just `A` and `B`.
say.bit: Several blanks: `<K, V>`. Each one can be a different type.

steps.title: In your lesson: More than one blank

say.never: `Pair<A, B>` holds two values that belong together: a team number and its nickname (`Pair<Integer, String>`), or a distance and a flywheel speed (`Pair<Double, Double>`). Its first value is type `A` and its second is type `B`.
say.bit: `Pair<A, B>`: a field of type A, one of type B, a constructor and two getters.

steps.title: In your lesson: A blank for a type

say.never: `RingBuffer<T>` keeps the last few things added, of any type: gyro headings (`RingBuffer<Double>`) or alerts (`RingBuffer<String>`). Inside, an `ArrayList<T>` holds them. When it's full, `add` removes the oldest one, at index 0, before adding the new one at the end. `get` and `latest` return a `T`.
say.bit: `RingBuffer<T>` stores an `ArrayList<T>`; `add` drops index 0 when full; `get` and `latest` return T.

marks.label: a list of whatever T is

say.never: Your turn! Add `<A, B>` after `Pair`, then the two fields, the constructor and `getFirst()` and `getSecond()`. After that, open `RingBuffer.java`, add `<T>` and write its methods.
